title: Common Encapsulation Mistakes
summary: Avoid dangerous anti-patterns: leaking mutable references, pseudo-encapsulation, and ignoring constructor validation.
learningOutcomes: Detect and prevent mutable reference leaks when returning arrays or objects
Understand why defensive copying preserves true encapsulation
Identify the 4 most common beginner encapsulation anti-patterns

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: Giving Away the Master Key by Accident

analogy.story:
Imagine a bank installs a massive 10-ton steel vault door with triple-combination locks. The bank manager strictly refuses to let any customer touch the vault door.

However, whenever a customer asks to see their safety deposit box, the manager hands them the physical Master Key to the entire vault and says: 'Here, take the key, look at your box, and bring the key back when you're done.'

A dishonest customer immediately duplicates the key. The 10-ton steel door is now completely useless!

This is exactly what happens when your encapsulated class returns a direct reference to a private mutable array or object: you built private walls, but handed out the master key to external code.
analogy.takeaway: Returning a reference to a mutable private field completely bypasses encapsulation. Always return a defensive copy or provide specific query methods.

activities.title: The 4 Major Encapsulation Anti-Patterns

concept.explanation:
Even experienced programmers fall into subtle traps that undermine encapsulation:

1. Leaking Mutable References: Returning an array (e.g., int[] getScores()) or a mutable object directly from a getter. The outside caller can modify elements in the array, mutating the class's private field directly!
   - Fix: Return a defensive clone or copy.

2. Accepting Mutable References in Constructors: Storing an incoming array or object directly without copying it. The caller can alter their local array and mutate the object from the outside.
   - Fix: Store a copy: this.scores = scores.clone().

3. Pseudo-Encapsulation: Making fields private, but immediately generating public getters and public setters for every single field with zero validation. This provides no protection over public fields.

4. Bypassing Validation in Constructors: Writing extensive checks in setAge(), but having the constructor do 'this.age = age;' directly, allowing newborn objects to bypass validation.
rules: Rule 1: Never return direct references to private mutable objects or arrays.
Rule 2: Never store direct references to caller-provided mutable arrays without copying.
Rule 3: Always route constructor assignments through validation logic.

keyTakeaways: Rule 1: Never return direct references to private mutable objects or arrays.
Rule 2: Never store direct references to caller-provided mutable arrays without copying.
Rule 3: Always route constructor assignments through validation logic.

questions.prompt: What is a 'mutable reference leak' in Java?
questions.question: What is a 'mutable reference leak' in Java?
options: A memory leak that causes the garbage collector to crash
Returning a direct reference to a private mutable object or array from a getter, allowing external callers to modify internal state directly
Declaring a variable as final and static
Forgetting to write a constructor
questions.explanation: A mutable reference leak happens when an encapsulated class exposes direct pointers to its internal mutable data structures.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent external callers from modifying a private array field when implementing a getter?
questions.question: How do you prevent external callers from modifying a private array field when implementing a getter?
options: Mark the getter method as private
Return a defensive clone (e.g. return scores.clone();) or provide indexed query methods
Convert the array to a String and back
Delete the array after reading
questions.explanation: Returning a clone gives the caller a distinct memory copy, so modifying elements in the copy has zero effect on the class's private field.

questions.prompt: What is 'pseudo-encapsulation'?
questions.question: What is 'pseudo-encapsulation'?
options: Writing code in C++ instead of Java
Marking fields private but blindly providing unrestricted public getters and setters for all of them with no validation
Using static methods inside abstract classes
Writing classes without packages
questions.explanation: Pseudo-encapsulation offers no real security or integrity because public setters with no validation are practically equivalent to public fields.

questions.prompt: If a constructor receives 'int[] data' from a caller and assigns 'this.data = data;', what is the danger?
questions.question: If a constructor receives 'int[] data' from a caller and assigns 'this.data = data;', what is the danger?
options: The compiler will fail
The caller retains their reference to 'data' and can modify elements at any time, mutating the internal state from the outside
The array size is doubled automatically
Memory is leaked permanently
questions.explanation: Both the caller and the object now point to the exact same array on the heap. The caller can mutate it at any time.

questions.prompt: Why is primitive data (int, double, boolean) immune to mutable reference leaks?
questions.question: Why is primitive data (int, double, boolean) immune to mutable reference leaks?
options: Because Java primitives are passed and returned by value (copied), not by reference
Because primitives are stored in the operating system
Because primitives cannot be made private
Because primitives are automatically final
questions.explanation: Java primitives are passed and returned by value; the recipient gets an independent copy of the bits, making leaks impossible.

questions.prompt: What is the common mistake when designing constructors in encapsulated classes?
questions.question: What is the common mistake when designing constructors in encapsulated classes?
options: Writing too many comments
Assigning parameter values directly into private fields without validating them, allowing invalid objects to be born
Using the this keyword
Making constructors public
questions.explanation: Constructors must validate incoming data just like setters do, otherwise objects can be instantiated in illegal states.

questions.prompt: In our Master Key analogy, what represents handing out the master key to visitors?
questions.question: In our Master Key analogy, what represents handing out the master key to visitors?
options: Making the class public
Returning a direct reference to a mutable internal array from a public getter
Printing logs to System.out
Calling super()
questions.explanation: Returning direct references to mutable internal structures allows outsiders to bypass the vault door entirely.

questions.prompt: Which of the following field types is safe to return from a getter WITHOUT a defensive copy?
questions.question: Which of the following field types is safe to return from a getter WITHOUT a defensive copy?
options: int[]
java.lang.String
java.util.Date
java.util.ArrayList
questions.explanation: String is an immutable class in Java. Its internal contents cannot be altered, so returning a reference to a String is 100% safe.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of providing indexed query methods (e.g. getScoreAt(int index)) instead of getScores()?
questions.question: What is the benefit of providing indexed query methods (e.g. getScoreAt(int index)) instead of getScores()?
options: It avoids creating and copying arrays entirely while keeping the underlying storage completely private
It makes array lookups slower
It allows scores to be negative
It makes the JVM compile faster
questions.explanation: Indexed query methods expose only single primitive values on demand, eliminating both reference leaks and copying overhead.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to handle constructor validation without duplicating code from setters?
questions.question: What is the best way to handle constructor validation without duplicating code from setters?
options: Delete the setters and only use constructors
Call the setter methods directly from within the constructor (e.g. setAge(age);)
Copy-paste the if statements into every constructor
Skip validation in constructors
questions.explanation: Invoking setters from constructors reuses validation logic and keeps code DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

questions.question: Explain what a defensive copy is and when you must use it.
questions.answer: A defensive copy is a duplicate copy of a mutable object created to protect internal state. You must use defensive copies in two scenarios: 1. In constructors/setters when accepting mutable objects from callers. 2. In getters when returning mutable internal objects (such as arrays or Dates) to callers.

questions.question: Why is java.lang.String safe to return from getters without defensive copying, while java.util.Date is not?
questions.answer: String is immutable—it has no methods to alter its internal character array once instantiated. In contrast, java.util.Date has mutable methods like setTime(), allowing callers to alter the timestamp of the internal object directly.

questions.question: What is 'pseudo-encapsulation' and why is it dangerous in domain-driven systems?
questions.answer: Pseudo-encapsulation occurs when an engineer makes fields private, but automatically generates unrestricted public getters and setters for all of them without business validation. It provides an illusion of protection while allowing external callers to corrupt domain invariants just as easily as public fields.
keyTakeaways: Private fields + unrestricted setters = illusion of security

questions.question: How can an API designer avoid returning arrays or collections altogether?
questions.answer: By providing granular querying and domain mutation methods (e.g. 'int getItemCount()', 'Item getItemAt(int index)', 'void addItem(Item item)') rather than exposing the entire raw collection. This preserves complete encapsulation and prevents caller tampering.
keyTakeaways: Provide granular queries instead of exposing raw collections

questions.question: Why is constructor-setter delegation preferable to direct field assignment in constructors?
questions.answer: Because business validation rules are maintained in a single place (the setter). If validation rules change in the future, updating the setter automatically updates both ongoing mutations and object construction, eliminating out-of-sync validation bugs.
keyTakeaways: Single source of truth for validation

questions.question: What is the performance overhead of defensive copying, and how can it be mitigated?
questions.answer: Defensive copying allocates new objects on the heap, increasing garbage collection load. It can be mitigated by returning immutable data structures, using primitive streams, or exposing indexed read methods rather than cloning full collections.
keyTakeaways: Mitigate with indexed queries or unmodifiable views

practiceProblems.title: Challenge: Safe Integer Matrix Envelope
practiceProblems.description: Write a complete SecureMatrix class from scratch with private int[][] grid (rows x cols). Constructor takes int rows, int cols and initializes grid. Provide setCell(int r, int c, int val) that bounds-checks r and c. Provide getCell(int r, int c) that returns cell value or -1 if out of bounds. DO NOT provide getGrid()! In Main, create 3x3 matrix, set (1, 1) to 99, try setting (5, 5) to 10 (safely ignored), and print 'Center cell: 99'.
